summary: Titus 3 moves from public conduct toward rulers and neighbors, to a compact account of God's mercy, renewal, and hope. It then contrasts useful good works with unprofitable quarrels and closes with travel plans, support for fellow workers, and greetings.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers the letter's main concern: mercy is not earned by righteous works, yet those who believe God are pressed toward work that benefits people and meets needs.

context.author: The letter names Paul as sender. Traditional Pauline authorship remains defended, while many scholars understand Titus as later writing within the Pauline tradition.
context.audience: Titus, with instructions concerning Christian communities on Crete; the final greeting addresses more than one person.
context.date: No year is secure. Direct Pauline authorship is commonly placed in the 60s CE, while later first-century or early second-century dates are proposed by others.
context.setting: Titus's assignment is Crete. In this chapter the sender plans to winter at Nicopolis, but the place of writing is not named.
context.literaryForm: A letter of delegated instruction, combining commands about conduct, a concentrated statement of salvation, warnings about disputes, and closing travel arrangements.

outline.heading: Public conduct toward rulers and everyone
outline.note: Titus is to remind the community to be subject, obedient, ready for good work, gentle, and humble toward all.

outline.heading: The former way of life
outline.note: The chapter explains gentleness by recalling that 'we' also once lived in folly, deception, malice, envy, and hatred.

outline.heading: Mercy, renewal, and hope
outline.note: God's kindness and love appear; salvation is described as mercy, washing, renewal by the Holy Spirit, justification by grace, and hope of eternal life.

outline.heading: Useful work instead of empty quarrels
outline.note: Believers are to maintain good works, while foolish controversies and a repeatedly warned factious person are to be avoided.

outline.heading: Travel plans and practical support
outline.note: The sender plans for Titus to come to Nicopolis and urges support for Zenas and Apollos so necessary needs are met.

outline.heading: Final greetings
outline.note: The letter closes with greetings to those who love the sender's circle in faith and a blessing of grace.

keyVerses.text: not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
keyVerses.why: This sentence states the chapter's central contrast: salvation is grounded in mercy, not in prior righteous deeds.

keyVerses.text: This saying is faithful, and concerning these things I desire that you insist confidently, so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable to men;
keyVerses.why: It connects belief with careful attention to good works and names their benefit for people.

keyVerses.text: but shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
keyVerses.why: This verse sets the opposite path beside good works: arguments that the chapter calls useless and empty.

keyVerses.text: Let our people also learn to maintain good works to meet necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful.
keyVerses.why: The closing instruction makes good works concrete: they meet real needs.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with rulers and authorities?
questions.answer: The chapter opens with instructions about public conduct. Titus is to remind the community to be subject to rulers and authorities, obedient, and ready for every good work. The next verse widens the concern beyond government to speech, gentleness, and humility toward all people.

questions.question: Does being in subjection mean every ruler is being approved?
questions.answer: The verse commands subjection and obedience, but it does not discuss every possible conflict between authority and conscience. It is part of a larger call to conduct that is ready for good work and marked by gentleness. The chapter's focus is public credibility and peaceable behavior, not a complete political theory.

questions.question: Why does verse 3 describe the readers' former life so sharply?
questions.answer: Verse 3 gives a reason for humility toward others: the community is reminded that 'we' also once lived in foolishness, disobedience, deception, malice, envy, hatred, and mutual hostility. The point is not to excuse those things, but to keep the readers from treating outsiders or opponents with contempt.

questions.question: What does 'washing of regeneration' mean here?
questions.answer: Regeneration means rebirth or renewal of life. The phrase joins washing with rebirth and places it beside renewal by the Holy Spirit. This imagery is commonly read in connection with baptism, while Christian traditions differ over how the rite relates to the renewal described. The saving action is attributed to God's mercy, not prior righteous deeds.

questions.question: Are good works the basis of salvation in this chapter?
questions.answer: No. Verse 5 says salvation is 'not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves' but according to God's mercy. Yet verses 8 and 14 still urge believers to maintain good works, so the chapter gives mercy and action different roles: mercy saves, and good works are the useful life expected afterward.

questions.question: What are the 'genealogies' and disputes about the law?
questions.answer: Verse 9 lists foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law, but gives no detailed account of their content. It contrasts these unprofitable quarrels with the beneficial work urged in verse 8. The instruction targets arguments described as empty and divisive; their precise teaching cannot be reconstructed from this list alone.

questions.question: What is a 'factious man'?
questions.answer: A factious person creates division in the setting of quarrels and disputes. The instruction calls for a first and second warning before avoidance. KJV and Douay-Rheims use forms of the word heretic, which can suggest later technical categories. Here the surrounding verses emphasize divisiveness, repeated warnings, and the person's persistence in wrongdoing.

questions.question: Why are Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas, and Apollos mentioned at the end?
questions.answer: They belong to the letter's practical travel arrangements. Artemas or Tychicus may be sent to Titus, after which Titus is to come to Nicopolis. Zenas and Apollos are to be helped on their journey so nothing is lacking for them.

questions.question: How does the closing instruction connect to the rest of the chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 14 repeats the call to maintain good works, but now ties it to necessary needs. That makes the chapter's language about profitable conduct concrete: the community is to learn practices that help people and keep them from being unfruitful.

glossary.def: People with governing authority; in this chapter the community is told to be in subjection to them and obedient.
Those who hold public authority; paired with rulers in the opening command about public conduct.
An image in verse 5 connected with regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit; it is commonly read in connection with baptism, though the verse emphasizes God's mercy.
A word in verse 5 for new birth or new beginning, joined to washing and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
A divisive person in the context of quarrels and disputes, to be avoided after a first and second warning.
The place where the sender says he has determined to spend the winter.
